speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you describe the appearance of your rash and tell me which antibiotic you were prescribed recently?

speaker: Patient
text: 8-year-old girl. The patient was brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of low-grade fever, itchy rash, and generalized joint pain. The rash initially started in the antecubital and popliteal fossae before spreading to the trunk and distal extremities. One week ago, she was diagnosed with acute sinusitis and started on amoxicillin. She has no history of adverse drug reactions, and her immunizations are up to date.

speaker: Doctor
text: Has the rash changed in appearance, such as becoming purplish or bruise-like, and has she experienced any abdominal pain or blood in her urine? I am evaluating for Henoch-Schönlein purpura, which can be triggered by infections or medications and presents with palpable purpura, arthralgia, and gastrointestinal involvement.

speaker: Doctor
text: Are the spots on her skin raised and do they blanch (turn white) when you press on them? Also, has she reported any stomach pain or noticed any swelling in her legs or around her eyes?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Diagnosed with acute sinusitis one week ago, no known history of adverse drug reactions, immunizations up to date. Social history: No significant social history provided.

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal urinalysis and CBC make Henoch-Schönlein purpura and other systemic vasculitides less likely. Given the timing after amoxicillin and the itchy, spreading nature of the rash, this is most consistent with a morbilliform drug eruption. DIAGNOSIS READY: Morbilliform Drug Eruption
